questions.q: List the three distinct supporting groups explicitly or implicitly presented across the three stanzas of the poem.
questions.a: The three groups are: (1) The pallbearers/procession carriers (Stanza 1: implied by "fpjkxk¡ gjsoQ ?kj osQ fy,"), (2) The dead person's relatives/mourners (Stanza 2: "cxhps"), and (3) The generalized world/society or onlookers (Stanza 3: "cgj"). A wrong answer that lists only "people" or "crowd" reveals the student cannot distinguish functional groups in a collective scene—a senior-secondary error where students treat all background figures as an undifferentiated mass rather than analyzing distinct social roles.

questions.q: Explain in your own words the difference between the grief of the "cxhps" (relatives) in Stanza 2 and the grief of the speaker ("eSa").
questions.a: The relatives' grief is described as "xqyeksgj osQ rys" (a heap/pile of sorrow)—external, accumulated, performative, and spatially located in their laps. The speaker's grief is "xSj dh xfy;ksa esa" (in the corners of the heart)—internal, hidden, residual, and spatially metaphorical. A wrong answer equating both as "sadness" reveals the student misses the poem's central contrast: performed/public ritual vs. authentic/private feeling. This is a Class 11-specific error where students ignore spatial metaphors ("rys" vs "xfy;k") that encode the thematic tension.

questions.q: The word "fpjkx" appears twice in Stanza 1 with different case endings ("fpjkxk¡" and "fpjkx"). Apply your knowledge of Hindi grammar and poetic ambiguity to explain how this double usage characterizes the pallbearers' attitude toward the dead body.
questions.a: First "fpjkxk¡" (nominative plural?/direct case) treats the body as an active agent being taken somewhere ("fpjkxk¡ gjsoQ ?kj osQ fy,"). Second "fpjkx" (oblique?/object) treats it as passive cargo ("fpjkx e;Llj ugha 'kgj osQ fy,"). The shift from subject to object mirrors the pallbearers' view: initially a person with a destination, ultimately a burden without agency. A wrong answer focusing only on dictionary meaning ("dead body") reveals inability to track grammatical shifts as characterization—a skill required for board-level poetic analysis.

questions.q: Analyze how the spatial arrangement of the three supporting groups across the stanzas (procession → relatives → world) creates a structural movement from physical proximity to metaphysical distance.
questions.a: Stanza 1: Pallbearers are physically touching the body ("gjsoQ ?kj osQ fy,"). Stanza 2: Relatives are adjacent ("cxhps esa") but emotionally performative. Stanza 3: "cgj" (world) is abstract, ruled by "fu”kke" (death/time), with the body reduced to harvest ("fly"). The movement is: intimate labor → familial performance → cosmic indifference. A wrong answer listing groups without spatial verbs ("gjsoQ", "esa", "fy,") reveals the student reads stanzas as isolated pictures rather than a deliberate spatial argument—a key board exam analytical skill.

questions.q: Evaluate whether the poet portrays the supporting characters with sympathy, irony, or condemnation. Defend your judgment using two specific textual markers.
questions.a: The portrayal is **ironic detachment**, not sympathy or condemnation. Evidence: (1) "u gks deh”k rks ik¡oksa ls isV <¡d ysaxs" (if not a funeral pyre, they'd pull grass for a living)—pallbearers' labor is economically interchangeable, stripping ritual sanctity with flat factuality. (2) "os eqrebu gSa fd iRFkj fi?ky ugha ldrk" (they are helpless, cannot face the truth)—relatives are "eqrebu" (helpless), not hypocritical; the poet pities their entrapment in social forms. A wrong answer claiming "criticism of hypocrites" reveals the student imposes moral judgment where the poem offers sociological observation—a common Class 11 error when students confuse irony with satire.

questions.q: Create a 4-line Hindi couplet (dohe style) from the perspective of a pallbearer who has carried hundreds of "fpjkx," revealing his inner thought that contrasts with his outward action.
questions.a: Example: "bohq gya fpjkx, koi na puchhe naam / kaam hai yahi mera, mile do waqt ka kaam." (Carried hundreds of bodies, none ask the name / This is my work, just get two meals a day.) A poor answer writes a generic sad poem about death, revealing the student cannot adopt a supporting character's *specific* voice shaped by economic compulsion and routine—they default to universal grief, missing the poem's class-conscious characterization.
